orders.description: Defendants’ limited appeal from order entered on or about July 2, 2019.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied dismissal of negligent ownership, management and maintenance cause of action.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped descending interior marble stairs with a worn tread in defendants’ building. Experts proposed insufficient slip resistance and causation, but their stated friction benchmark was not shown to be an accepted industry standard.

legal_issues.finding: Worn marble tread alone was not an actionable defect; opposition did not establish an additional actionable condition.
Experts’ opinions about the cause of slipping were speculative.
Friction benchmark not shown to be accepted industry standard and expert causal opinions speculative; affidavits raised no triable issue.
Plaintiff abandoned moisture-maintenance claim and could not revive moisture as an actionable condition on appeal.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s experts supplied affidavits addressing friction and slip causation, found insufficient.

quality.notes: Review private-property status: defendants’ building lacks explicit ownership/private use; claim label is not proof of title. Worn tread alone held nonactionable, not a measured trivial-defect ruling. Moisture theory abandoned; industry friction standard not statutory code.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Wilma Guzman, J.), entered on or about July 2, 2019, which, insofar as appealed from as limited by the briefs, denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the cause of action alleging negligent ownership, management and maintenance of the premises, unanimously reversed, on the law, without costs, the motion granted, and the complaint dismissed. The Clerk is directed to enter judgment accordingly.
where plaintiff was injured when, while descending interior stairs in defendants' building, she slipped and fell on a marble step that had a worn tread.
A worn marble tread, without more, is not an actionable defect

Having abandoned her claim that defendants were negligent in keeping the stairs free of moisture, plaintiff cannot now argue that the existence of moisture on the stairs would be an actionable condition.

Nor did plaintiff's experts establish that in addition to the worn marble stair treads, they lacked adequate slip resistance, as the coefficient of friction value that the experts used as a standard value was not shown to be an accepted industry standard
Nor did the experts' affidavits raise a triable issue of fact, since the opinions concerning the cause of plaintiff's slip were speculative

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal deemed taken from June 2, 2015 judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Dismissed complaint upon April 17, 2015 summary-judgment order.

facts.factual_summary: Tenant allegedly slipped on accumulated bathroom water in her apartment on November 8, 2012, attributing it to a malfunctioning toilet. She had complained about a noisy, stiff handle months earlier but not floor water; defendants described adjusting the handle without observing leakage.

legal_issues.finding: Deposition evidence established noncreation; defendants had replaced no toilet/tank parts and handle adjustment was not linked to leakage.
No prior water/leak complaints or observed leakage; defendants established lack of actual notice and plaintiff raised no issue.
General awareness of handle trouble did not establish notice of the particular water condition; plaintiff saw no water until after falling.
Notice of appeal from order deemed to reference ensuing judgment under CPLR 5512(a).

evidence_discussed.description: Parties’ deposition excerpts addressed unseen water, handle complaints/adjustment and absence of known leakage.

quality.notes: One judgment on appeal; underlying order not separate appealed unit. Toilet-handle complaint and adjustment did not establish notice of floor water. Plaintiff’s alleged malfunction source not conclusively found.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the judgment is affirmed, with costs.

On November 8, 2012, the plaintiff, a tenant in a two-family house on Staten Island owned by the defendants, allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell due to an accumulation of water on the bathroom floor of her apartment. According to the plaintiff, the water accumulation was caused by a malfunctioning toilet.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from a judgment of the Supreme Court, Richmond County, entered June 2, 2015, which, upon an order of the same court (Troia, J.) dated April 17, 2015, granting the defendants’ motion for summary judgment, dismissed the complaint.
The notice of appeal from the order is deemed to be a notice of appeal from the judgment

Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that they neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the alleged water condition that caused the plaintiff to fall and sustain injuries (see Chudinova v Kleyner, 130 AD3d 859 [2015]; Taylor v Jaslove, 61 AD3d 743 [2009]; Alvarez v American Intl. Realty Corp., 60 AD3d 793 [2009]). In support of their motion, the defendants submitted excerpts from the plaintiff’s deposition transcript indicating that she did not see any water on the bathroom floor when she entered, and she only noticed it after she fell because her nightgown was wet. Moreover, although the plaintiff complained to the defendant Marcelle Rizkalla in June 2012 about the toilet handle making noise and being hard to push, at no time prior to her fall did she complain to the defendants about water on the bathroom floor.

The defendants also submitted excerpts from their deposition transcripts in which they demonstrated that they never *1105 changed any parts to the toilet or its tank, and that prior to this occurrence, the plaintiff never complained about any water on the bathroom floor or any leakage from the toilet. Further, while the defendant Marcelle Rizkalla adjusted the toilet handle a few months before the plaintiff’s accident, she never observed any water leaking onto the bathroom floor.

In opposition to the defendants’ prima facie showing, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact (see Taylor v Jaslove, 61 AD3d at 744 ). The defendants’ general awareness of a potential problem with the toilet handle was not sufficient to establish constructive notice of the particular condition which caused the plaintiff to fall
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from November 3, 2017 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted dismissal branch for lack of legal capacity to sue.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on defendant’s premises on April 23, 2013. The opinion provides no mechanism, hazard or precise location details.

legal_issues.finding: Undisclosed existing injury claim in Chapter 7 petition deprived plaintiff of capacity; defendant proved she knew or should have known of claim and opposition raised no issue. Judicial estoppel not reached.

evidence_discussed.description: Bankruptcy petition omitted injury cause already asserted; omission undisputed.

quality.notes: Procedural-only capacity ruling excludes case regardless of unspecified property status. No negligence merits, hazard, location, use or ownership inferred from corporate caption. Judicial estoppel expressly not reached.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
On April 23, 2013, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell while on the defendant's premises.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Thomas D. Raffaele, J.), dated November 3, 2017. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

On October 1, 2015, the plaintiff filed a petition under chapter 7 of the United States Bankruptcy Code. The petition was subsequently dismissed in May 2016. In February 2017, the defendant moved for, inter alia, summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground that the plaintiff lacked the legal capacity to sue.

Here, it is undisputed that the plaintiff did not disclose, in the bankruptcy petition that she filed in October 2015, the existence of the cause of action to recover damages for personal injuries that she had previously asserted against the defendant. The defendant established, prima facie, that when the petition was filed, the plaintiff knew or should have known of the existence of her cause of action, and the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact in opposition to that prima facie showing

Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination granting that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground that the plaintiff lacked the legal capacity to sue.
In light of our determination, we need not address the parties' contentions regarding the doctrine of judicial estoppel.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell while bowling in a bowling alley owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (K. Murphy, J.), entered March 17, 2016, which granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by submitting, inter alia, the deposition testimony of the plaintiff, which demonstrated that the plaintiff was unable to identify the cause of her fall
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from April 8, 2008 order resolving both defendants’ motions.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted separate owner and sweeping-contractor motions dismissing complaint against each.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped over a wire coat hanger in Rouse SI’s parking lot. Rouse SI hired ABCO to sweep the lot at night.

legal_issues.finding: ABCO established limited sweeping contract imposed no duty to plaintiff, and opposition raised no issue.
Owner established noncreation and lack of actual/constructive notice; opposition raised no triable issue.
Owner established noncreation and lack of actual/constructive notice; opposition raised no triable issue.
Owner met initial burden; appreciable duration of hanger on ground would be speculative.
Limited nighttime sweeping contract did not establish tort duty to plaintiff; no Espinal exception issue raised sufficiently.

evidence_discussed.description: Limited parking-lot sweeping contract addressed in contractor-duty analysis; text does not reproduce terms beyond limited task.

quality.notes: One appealed order deciding separate motions; wholly affirmed, not multiple orders/mixed. Direct negligence claim against contractor qualifies alongside owner claim. No retail use inferred from owner name; no particular sweeping performance or evidence format supplied.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with one bill of costs to the respondents.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped over a wire coat hanger in a parking lot owned by the defendant Rouse SI Shopping Center, LLC (hereinafter Rouse SI). Thereafter, she commenced this action against, among others, Rouse SI and the defendant ABCO Maintenance, Inc. (hereinafter ABCO), a company hired by Rouse SI to sweep the parking lot at night.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Richmond County (McMahon, J.), dated April 8, 2008, which granted the separate motions of the defendants Rouse SI Shopping Center, LLC, and ABCO Maintenance, Inc., for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.

Rouse SI established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that it neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the condition alleged by the plaintiff to have caused the accident
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to submit evidence sufficient to raise a triable issue of fact.
Any finding that the coat hanger had been on the ground for an appreciable period of time sufficient to charge Rouse SI with constructive notice would be speculative

Furthermore, in response to ABCO’s prima facie showing that it assumed no duty to the plaintiff by virtue of its limited contract with Rouse SI to sweep the parking lot, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to the existence of a duty
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the separate motions of Rouse SI and ABCO for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.
